latin.1826: XXVI. Atque hanc Scholasticorum veterum sententiam, hoc saeculo renovavit, & illustrare conatus est Cornelius Jansenius Episcopus Iprensis, ut videre est in volumine illo cui titulum fecit Augustinus, toto libro sexto de Gratia Christi Salvatoris. Ibi enim prolixe docet libertatem non opponi necessitati cuilibet, sed illi soli quae est a vi externa contra agentis inclinationem, quam coactionem dicimus. Idque quoniam in eo qui ex judicio rationis agit, sola coactio libertatem tollit, non autem necessitas inevitabilitatis & immutabilitatis. Adeoque agens liberum oppositum non esse agenti necessario, sicut nec opposita sunt agens naturale, & agens contingenter, sed agens liberum oppositum esse soli agenti naturali, quemadmodum agens contingenter oppositum est soli agenti necessario. Proinde non magis repugnare ut qui libere agit necessario agat, quam repugnat ut quod per naturam agit, agat etiam contingenter; quia sicut causa naturalis ab alia causa potest in agendo impediri, ita causa libera in agendo potest esse ad unum determinata immobiliter & immutabiliter.
latin.1827: XXVII. Porro libere juxta ipsum agit, quod ex judicio rationis agit, ac proinde cum voluntas sit appetitus rationalis, existimat voluntatem & naturam esse plane oppositas, neque magis voluntatem agere posse per modum naturae, quam naturam per modum causae liberae. Ideoque sicut nulla actio causae naturalis potest esse libera, ita quoque nullam actionem voluntatis posse naturalem esse, & non liberam: ac proinde liberum aeque late patere atque voluntarium, & quicquid voluntarium est eo ipso liberum esse; quia voluntas semper & essentialiter servat proprium suum operandi modum a natura distinctum.
latin.1828: XXVIII. Nihilominus agnoscit motus quosdam in voluntate oriri qui propterea tamen liberi non sunt: illos, scilicet, improvisos qui plenum rationis judicium praeveniunt, & qui motus primo primi vocari solent. Quanquam enim ex voluntate sine violentia fluant, deest tamen illis quod est in libertate praecipuum ex ejus sententia, quia in hominis potestate non sunt, & fiunt sine plena rationis advertentia, & invita quodammodo ac repugnante voluntate, quia dum in motus illos reflectitur, eis non consentit, & eos omnino nollet sibi inesse. De Gratia Christi Salvatoris lib. 6. cap. 37.
latin.1829: XXIX. Itaque juxta viri illius principia, dicendum est voluntarium bifariam accipi posse. Et 1. quidem sensu quodam latiori & minus proprio, prout complectitur omnes motus qui quacunque ratione in voluntate oriuntur, & ita voluntarium latius patet quam liberum; quoniam isto sensu motus primo primi voluntarii sunt, neque tamen liberi. 2. Stricte & proprie. Et sic voluntarii sunt illi omnes & soli voluntatis actus, qui ratione advertente, & re considerata judicium ferente, fiunt. Et ita voluntarium cum libero convertitur, neque illo Latius patet. Ac proinde cum voluntas non sine pleno & certo rationis judicio feratur in finem ultimum, non minus libere circa illum versatur quam dum appetit media, quae ad finem illum ducere videntur. Neque tantum homines in hac vita degentes, dum beati esse volunt, & nolunt esse miseri, liberum actum voluntatis edunt; sed ipsi quoque in coelo beati, dum tota voluntate Deo clare viso adhaerent, quoniam in utrisque voluntas fixum, certum & evidens constanterque probatum intellectus judicium hac in parte sequitur, & dum in se reflectitur ipsa, suum illum actum quam maxime probat.
latin.1830: XXX. Si quidem ad communem libertatis rationem, & propriam ejus essentiam, pertinere non existimat voluntatis quandam indifferentiam, & indeterminationem respectu actus qui liber dicitur, per quam voluntas possit contrarium agere, aut saltem actum illum omittere, vel suspendere. Quippe ex ejus mente, libertas solum in eo consistit, quod agens liberum sibi & actui suo dominetur, & seipsum agat & moveat, non autem ab alio agatur & moveatur, quod locum habere contendit etiam in iis actibus, ad quos voluntas determinata est necessario & immutabiliter.
latin.1831: XXXI. Etenim quae tum reperitur in voluntate necessitas, ut verbis Scoti mentem suam exprimit, non est praevia ad voluntatem, ut voluntas intelligatur cadere sub necessitate, tanquam impellente in actum, & figente in actum, quoniam si sic esset, voluntas ageretur & non ageret, nec staret in tali actu libertas. Sed est necessitas concomitans, ita quod ipsa intelligatur cadere sub voluntate, sic quod voluntas, propter firmitatem libertatis suae, sibi ipsi necessitatem imponit in eliciendo actum, & in perseverando, sive figendo, se in actum. De Grat. Chr. Salvat. lib. 6. cap. 37.
latin.1832: XXXII. Atque ut clarius ostendat agens rationale in omnibus quae vult & appetit, seipsum quodammodo agere & movere, etsi actus voluntatis ejus necessarius sit & immutabilis, observat potestatem agendi & movendi se, quae est agentis liberi propria, in eo sitam esse, quod tum ratio, tum voluntas, ad quas facultates libertas pertinet, super suos actus se reflectere possint; ita ut ratio possit de proprio suo judicio judicare, num recte judicaverit; & similiter voluntas non solum possit velle & appetere, sed ipsam quoque suam volitionem, suumque appetitum velle. Et quia in omni rationali motu, sive necessarius sit, sive non necessarius, semper adest tacite, vel expresse, hujusmodi super se reflexio, semper etiam in omni suo motu agens rationale seipsum movet & dominatur sibi, & ita propriam libertatem exercet.
latin.1833: XXXIII. Nam juxta ipsum, verae libertatis propria indicia sunt facere quod agenti lubet, quod ei placet, quod ei videtur. Unde colligit Beatos in coelo in diligendo Deum, quem clare vident, perfectissime seipsos movere, & perfectissimum sui actus dominium habere, & ita liberrimos esse, quia plenissimo & tranquillissimo judicio judicant sibi diligendum esse Deum, & in eo se sanissime judicare judicant; eorum vero voluntas amando, rationem sequi vult, & hoc se velle vult, ac cessare non vult. Quae vero necessitas in actu illo apparet, ab ipsa voluntate, & Dominii ac libertatis ejus perfectione proficiscitur, quia ipsa sibi necessitatem facit, non per modum naturae, sed perfectissimae libertatis, movendo & determinando se.
latin.1834: XXXIV. Caeterum quanquam Doctor ille ad propriam libertatis essentiam pertinere nolit ut voluntas ad suos actus indifferenter se habeat, ita nempe ut possit agere, & non agere, hoc vel etiam contrarium agere; tamen cum veteribus Scholasticis aperte fatetur talem indifferentiam hominum viatorum voluntati adesse; eorum enim libertatem non solum expertem esse coactionis, sed etiam necessitatis immutabilis voluntariae, hoc est, eam ad utrumque indifferentem esse. Id solum negat in illa indifferentia sitam esse generalem humani arbitrii libertatem. Quippe hanc indifferentiam certissimum quidem esse in creatura rationali libertatis indicium, non tamen libertatis esse causam, vel rationem. Et propterea adesse vel abesse posse voluntatis arbitrio, sine dispendio libertatis. De Gratia Chr. Salvat. lib. 6. cap. 34.
latin.1835: XXXV. Atque hanc Jansenii doctrinam amplexi sunt, & etiamnum amplectuntur qui se discipulos Augustini vocant, & ab adversariis dicuntur Jansenistae, ut videre est in libro cui titulum fecerunt, Manuale Catholicorum, Thesi Apologetica & dogmatica Vigesima prima. Ubi haec sunt eorum verba, Essentia libertatis nullo modo consistit in indifferentia. Nam ex Sanctis Patribus, Ubi voluntas ibi libertas. Est enim Liberum Arbitrium ex Sancto Prospero, Rei sibi placitae Spontaneus appetitus. Et ex S. Damasceno Arbitrii Libertas nihil aliud est quam voluntas. Et Paulo post, Quod voluntarie fit, etiamsi necessario fiat, libere tamen fit. Deus namque seipsum necessario amat, & tamen libere. Item, sola itaque necessitas coactionis, aut violentiae repugnat Libertati, non autem necessitas simplex, immutabilis, seu naturalis inclinationis.
latin.1836: XXXVI. In illo vero scripto quod vocant trium columnarum, ubi distinguunt varios sensus quinque famosarum propositionum, quas damnarunt Pontifices Romani Innocentius X. & Alexander VII. tertiae propositioni hunc sensum tanquam bonum & sibi probatum tribuunt. Ad merendum & demerendum, in statu naturae lapsae, non requiritur in homine libertas a necessitate infallibilitatis, sed sufficit Libertas a coactione cum judicio rationis, si consideretur praecise essentia libertatis & meriti, quanquam ex ratione status semper reperiatur indifferentia potentiae, qua voluntas, etiam sub gratia proxime necessaria & ex se efficaci potest non velle, non tamen ut unquam simul cum eadem gratia non velit. Ubi agnoscunt semper in statu naturae lapsae, Libertati adjunctam esse voluntatis indifferentiam. Et propterea in articulis illis Convenarum Episcopo oblatis, non verentur dicere, Quod ad merendum & demerendum in statu naturae lapsae non sufficit Libertas a coactione; sed requiritur libertas a necessitate. Quamvis enim, inquiunt, gratia per se efficax infallibiliter & insuperabiliter voluntatem ad agendum determinet, atque ita nunquam voluntas illi actu dissentiat; non tamen inducit necessitatem, quia non tollit dissentiendi potestatem.
latin.1837: XXXVII. Verum ista sententia quae libertatem arbitrii statuit oppositam esse, non necessitati, sed coactioni tantum; a Pontificibus Romanis damnata est. Nam Bellarminus meminit decreti cujusdam Pii V. quod postea a Gregorio XIII. renovatum fuit, in quo inter alias multas propositiones, hae quoque censura notantur. Quod voluntarie fit, etiamsi necessitate fiat, libere tamen fit. Item, sola violentia repugnat libertati hominis naturali.
latin.1838: XXXVIII. Idcirco Scholae Romanae communis hodie doctrina est, ad libertatem arbitrii non sufficere solam immunitatem a coactione, sed praeterea requiri immunitatem a necessitate, saltem absoluta atque naturali, qua res sunt per naturam ad unum determinatae, & simpliciter non possunt aliter agere quam agunt. Atque in hoc capite conveniunt tam illi qui recentiores Thomistae, quam qui Molinistae vocantur.
latin.1839: XXXIX. Itaque quod voluntarium est liberum esse nolunt, si voluntas sit ad illud necessario determinata, ut Beatorum Spirituum voluntas ad diligendum Deum quem clare vident. Ac proinde voluntarium concipiunt tanquam genus quoddam, quod sub se duas species complectatur, videlicet liberum quod fit cum delectu & praelectione, & voluntarium stricte & proprie sic dictum, quod fit quidem libenter, non tamen libere; quia necessario & immutabiliter. Voluntarii vero genus faciunt spontaneum, quoniam sponte agunt non tantum ea quae sunt intellectu & voluntate praedita, sed etiam bruta quae ratione carent. Imo & ipsa inanima, ut lapis quum deorsum tendit. Nam sponte agere est naturae impulsu agere.
latin.1840: XL. Itaque libentiam, sive complacentiam distinguunt a libertate: nec volunt ullam esse libertatem proprie dictam, nisi eam quae sit, vel contrarietatis, seu specificationis, per quam aliquis potest circa idem objectum elicere actus contrarios, vel appetere objecta contraria sive disparata. Vel saltem contradictionis, sive exercitii, per quam possit aliquis agere, & actionem suam suspendere, sive inhibere.
latin.1841: XLI. Nec enim volunt libertatem esse sine quadam agentis liberi ad agendum indifferentia & indeterminatione; & eos solos actus liberos esse putant quorum contrarium facere possumus, aut saltem eos omittere, & ab iis cessare: juxta vulgarem illam libertatis descriptionem, per quam in eo consistere dicitur quod agens liberum positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis possit agere, vel non agere, hoc, aut illud agere.
latin.1842: XLII. Observant tamen nonnulli Thomistae recentiores indifferentiam ad agendum, vel non agendum, esse quidem libertatis humanae proprietatem, quae ab illa separari nequit; verum in ea libertatis essentiam non consistere; sed potius in independentia, & eminentia supra bona finita, & vi illa regendi; sive in dominio quodam, quo se suaque ad ultimum finem referat. Ut videre est apud nuperum scriptorem Vincentium Baronium Dominicanum in tertia parte Theologiae dogmaticae; de Libertatis humanae & scientiae Dei principiis adversus Theophilum Raynaudum Jesuitam. Disp. 1. Artic. 3. §. 1. Sed juxta communiora hodiernae Scholae placita, ipsa libertatis essentia constituenda est in ista ad agendum, vel non agendum indifferentia.
latin.1843: XLIII. Porro Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae per indifferentiam illam quae libertatis essentiam, vel constituit, vel saltem necessario sequitur, significare nolunt eum voluntatis statum in quo inter duo opposita nutat, neque ad unum magis inclinat quam ad alterum; sed in aequilibrio quodammodo suspensa, paulo momento huc & illuc impellitur. Agnoscunt enim libertatem in eo reperiri qui ad agendum eo sensu minime est indifferens; sed cujus voluntas alte impressis habitibus ad certas actiones vehementer inclinata est, quique firmum propositum habet sic & non aliter agendi, a quo non nisi aegre admodum dimoveri potest. Sed indifferentia illa in qua, ex eorum mente, sita est arbitrii libertas, non aliud est quam vera potestas agendi & non agendi, quae manet etiam in eo qui fixo & constanti mentis, & voluntatis proposito ad agendum determinatus est.
latin.1844: XLIV. Praeterea observandum est, ex communi Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae sensu, ad libertatem non requiri indeterminationem & indifferentiam ad bene, vel male agendum. Nec esse de libertatis ratione posse bene operari, & multo minus adhuc posse male operari. Agnoscunt enim Deum esse agens liberrimum, qui tamen male agere non potest: ut nec potuit unquam Christus homo: neque jam possunt angeli, & spiritus coelestes qui, ex singulari Dei beneficio, sunt immutabiliter in bono confirmati, nec propterea tamen minus liberi sunt. Contra vero, iis fatentibus, Cacodaemones & Spiritus damnatorum in inferno nihil boni agere possunt, & tamen libere agunt, ac in iis mansit liberum arbitrium. Idque quoniam, licet illi ad bene agendum, & hi contra ad male agendum determinati sint, possunt tamen ab his & illis actibus abstinere, & inter plura bona, vel mala eligere. Ut videre est apud Puteanum in 1. 2. quaest. 10. art. 1, 2, 3, 4. dubit. 3. Et apud Gulielmum Estium in 2. sent. dist. 14. §. 5.
latin.1845: XLV. Caeterum descriptio illa in qua libertas dicitur esse id per quod, positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, agens liberum potest agere, & non agere, hoc & illud agere, non eodem sensu exponitur ab omnibus Scholae Romanae Theologis. Quod ut intelligatur, notandum est verbis istis posse tribui multiplicem sensum. Et primo quidem verba illa ita possunt accipi quasi iis significaretur agens liberum posse agere & non agere simul, & eodem tempore contrarios actus exercere. Hic sensus tanquam manifeste falsus ab omnibus rejicitur. Fatentur enim omnes in agente libero simul compati non posse actum & cessationem ab actu, aut unum actum & ejus contrarium; ac proinde verbis illis aliud non significari, quam quod agens liberum simul habet potestatem ad actus contrarios, & quod simul in eo reperitur potestas agendi, & potestas quoque non agendi; quod in Scholis dicitur per hoc agenti libero tribui simultatem potentiae, non potentiam simultatis.
latin.1846: XLVI. Secundo vero hujus descriptionis hic sensus esse potest, quod positis omnibus quae praerequiruntur ad actum aliquem voluntatis liberae, tam ex parte objecti, quam ex parte Dei, & intellectus ipsius, possit actus ille tam non sequi quam sequi, & etiam contrarius actus in ejus locum substitui: ita ut, quamvis componi & conjungi non possint actus aliquis & ejus privatio, vel contrarius actus; tamen cum omnibus illis quae praerequiruntur ad aliquem actum Humanae voluntatis verbi causa, conversionis, & dilectionis Dei, conjungi possit, & saepe de facto conjungatur, illius actus privatio, & actus etiam illi oppositus: Et sic, non obstante quocunque objecti lumine, & etiam illecebra, quocunque dictamine & judicio intellectus, ac denique quacunque divina motione, quae impellant ad conversionem, & tamen actualem voluntatis ipsius determinationem praecedant, possit reapse conversio non sequi; & saepe de facto contingat, ista omnia pari modo se habentia, in uno quidem habere junctam conversionem, in alio vero minime, propterea quod voluntas in uno se sic determinavit, in alio vero secus.
latin.1847: XLVII. Atque hic sensus probatur & admittitur ab iis, qui in Schola Romana Molinistae dicuntur. Nec enim volunt quicquam esse eorum quae tam ex parte Dei, quam ex parte intellectus, voluntatem humanam ad consensum praeparant, & antecedenter movent atque impellunt, cum quo stare non possit voluntatis dissensus. Ac statuunt quodlibet rationis judicium, & quamlibet etiam divinam motionem, componi posse, non solum cum actu ad quem voluntatem praemovent & dirigunt, sed etiam cum actus illius carentia, imo cum actu contrario: adeo ut eadem gratiae divinae motio in uno conversionem ad Deum operetur, in alio vero non: propterea quod unus gratiae divinae ductum ultro sequi voluit, alter vero minime. Et ita diverso respectu & negant & affirmant, agens liberum positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, posse, in sensu composito, agere & non agere, hoc & illud agere. Si quis enim intelligat in agente libero componi posse actum & cessationem ab actu, actum unum & ejus oppositum, fatentur sensum illum compositum falsum esse, & solum sensum divisum, qui illi opponitur, verum. Siquis vero pertendat non quidem cum actu ipso, sed tamen cum omnibus ad agendum requisitis, componi posse privationem actus, & actum oppositum, sensus ille compositus, juxta illos, verus est.
latin.1848: XLVIII. Verum aliter sentiunt qui dicuntur Thomistae recentiores. Nam juxta eorum doctrinam, uterque ille sensus compositus falsus est. Siquidem putant non solum cum actu jungi non posse ejus privationem, aut actum oppositum; sed ne quidem cum iis quae sunt ad agendum praerequisita, inter quae locum habet divina quaedam praemotio, consistere posse negationem actus, & multo minus actum contrarium. Idque quia positis quae praerequiruntur ad aliquem actum, actus ille sequitur certo & infallibiliter; nec unquam contingere potest ut non sequatur. Et tamen concedunt, positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, agens liberum posse agere, atque non agere, hoc & illud agere: quia licet cum istis praerequisitis stare non possit actus negatio, vel suspensio actus; optime tamen cum iis consistit potestas non agendi, sive etiam contrarium agendi. Non secus ac cum actuali voluntatis consensu stare quidem nequit voluntatis dissensus, sed tamen manet ipsa dissentiendi potestas: Et cum actu sedendi compati non potest ambulandi actus, quamvis illi non repugnet potestas ambulandi, quae in sedente per actum sedendi non tollitur. Eo igitur modo praerequisita ad agendum, tum ex parte Dei, tum ex parte intellectus nostri, actum ipsum secum per consequentiam necessariam trahunt, & tamen potestatem non agendi minime tollunt. Quoniam efficiunt quidem ut voluntas agat, sed ita tamen agat, ut possit non agere, & aliter agendi potestatem non amittat.
latin.1849: XLIX. Sic mentem suam hac de re exponit Didacus Alvares Archiepiscopus Tranensis & Salpensis, inter recentiores Thomistas praecipuus. Dicendum est, inquit, ad libertatem arbitrii necessario requiri, quod positis omnibus antecedenter secundum ordinem rationis vel temporis ad actum praerequisitis possit operari, vel non operari, ita videlicet, ut cum iisdem praerequisitis stet simul in libero arbitrio facultas & potentia, qua possit operari, vel non operari, si velit. Et probatur, Nam si aliquod ex praerequisitis ad operandum talem actum in particulari tolleret a libero arbitrio facultatem, seu potentiam ad non operandum, vel ad operandum actum oppositum; id efficeret motio Dei efficax, qua ad talem actum praedeterminatur: sed hujusmodi motio non tollit a libero arbitrio facultatem non operandi illum actum, vel operandi actum contrarium, sed solum efficit, quod cum liberum arbitrium possit operari, & non operari talem actum; infallibiliter tamen & libere operetur illum.... Non tamen est de ratione, aut definitione liberi arbitrii, quod positis omnibus, secundum ordinem causalitatis antecedenter praerequisitis, ad operandum talem actum, possit eundem actum non operari in sensu composito, si compositio fiat inter ejusmodi praerequisita, & carentiam talis actus, seu actum contrarium. Itaque haec duo simul sunt incompossibilia, quod scilicet, in libero arbitrio, pro aliquo instanti temporis, sint omnia antecedenter praerequisita secundum ordinem causalitatis, ad productionem talis actus, & non producat illum sed producat actum contrarium. Et nihilominus cum hac impossibilitate stat simul libertas arbitrii. In summa operis de auxiliis Divinae gratiae lib. 4. cap. 14. num. 5. & 6. Ideoque ad vitandam omnem aequivocationem, haec est, juxta ipsum, liberi arbitrii legitima definitio, liberum arbitrium est facultas voluntatis, & rationis ad utrumlibet agendum, vel non agendum, & agendum unum, vel alterum.

sections.title: Jansenius revives the old scholastic view: freedom opposed only to compulsion
sections.pass_a: And this opinion of the old Scholastics Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres, renewed in this age, and endeavoured to illustrate, as may be seen in that volume to which he gave the title Augustinus, in the whole sixth book on the Grace of Christ the Saviour. For there he teaches at length that liberty is not opposed to every necessity, but to that alone which is from external force against the inclination of the agent, which we call compulsion. And that because in him who acts from the judgment of reason, compulsion alone takes away liberty, not however the necessity of inevitability and immutability. And so the free agent is not opposed to the necessary agent, just as the natural agent and the agent contingently are not opposed, but the free agent is opposed to the natural agent alone, as the agent contingently is opposed to the necessary agent alone. Accordingly it is no more repugnant that he who acts freely should act necessarily, than it is repugnant that what acts by nature should also act contingently; because as a natural cause can be hindered in acting by another cause, so a free cause can in acting be determined to one thing immovably and immutably.
pass_b: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, revived this view of the old scholastics in our own time and tried to explain it, as can be seen throughout the sixth book, on the grace of Christ the Saviour, of the volume he called Augustinus.

There he argues at length that freedom is opposed not to every necessity but only to the one that comes from outside force working against the agent's inclination, which we call compulsion. In someone who acts on the judgment of reason, he says, compulsion alone removes freedom; the necessity of inevitability and immutability does not.

So a free agent is not the opposite of a necessary agent, any more than a natural agent is the opposite of one acting contingently. The free agent is opposed only to the natural agent, just as the contingent agent is opposed only to the necessary one.

Therefore it is no more contradictory for one who acts freely to act necessarily than for something acting by nature to act contingently. A natural cause can be hindered in its action by another cause, and in the same way a free cause can be fixed on one course immovably and unchangeably.

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.

notes: Cornelius Jansenius, Augustinus (1640), tom. 3, De gratia Christi Salvatoris, lib. 6.

sections.title: Jansenius: whatever is voluntary is free, since will and nature are opposite principles
sections.pass_a: Further, according to him that acts freely which acts from the judgment of reason, and accordingly since the will is a rational appetite, he thinks the will and nature to be plainly opposed, and that the will can no more act by way of nature, than nature by way of a free cause. And therefore just as no action of a natural cause can be free, so also no action of the will can be natural, and not free: and accordingly that the free extends as widely as the voluntary, and whatever is voluntary is by that very fact free; because the will always and essentially keeps its own proper mode of operating distinct from nature.
pass_b: For Jansenius, whatever acts on the judgment of reason acts freely. Since the will is a rational appetite, he holds that will and nature are flatly opposed, and that the will can no more act in the manner of nature than nature can act in the manner of a free cause.

Just as no action of a natural cause can be free, so no action of the will can be natural rather than free. The free therefore reaches exactly as far as the voluntary, and whatever is voluntary is free by that very fact, because the will always and by its essence keeps its own way of acting, distinct from that of nature.

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.

sections.title: Jansenius grants first impulses of the will are not free, because not in man's power
sections.pass_a: Nevertheless he acknowledges that certain motions arise in the will which nevertheless are not free on that account: those, namely, unforeseen ones which anticipate the full judgment of reason, and which are wont to be called first-first motions. For although they flow from the will without violence, yet there is lacking in them that which in his opinion is chief in liberty, because they are not in man's power, and come about without full advertence of reason, and with the will in some way unwilling and resisting, because while it reflects upon those motions, it does not consent to them, and would altogether not wish them to be in it. On the Grace of Christ the Saviour book 6. chap. 37.
pass_b: He does admit that some motions arise in the will that are not free for all that. These are the sudden ones that run ahead of reason's full judgment, usually called 'first-first motions'.

They come from the will without violence, yet they lack what he takes to be the chief thing in freedom. They are not in a man's power, they happen without reason's full attention, and they happen even against the will's wishes and resistance in some way, since when the will reflects on them it does not consent and would rather not have them in it at all. (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 37.)

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.

notes: motus primo primi: the scholastic term for involuntary first stirrings of desire that precede deliberation.

sections.title: The voluntary in a broad and a strict sense; in the strict sense it converts with the free, even in the blessed
sections.pass_a: Therefore according to that man's principles, it must be said that the voluntary can be taken in two ways. And 1. indeed in a certain wider and less proper sense, as it embraces all motions which in whatever way arise in the will, and so the voluntary extends more widely than the free; since in that sense first-first motions are voluntary, and yet not free. 2. Strictly and properly. And so all those and only those acts of the will are voluntary which take place with reason adverting, and passing judgment on the thing considered. And so the voluntary is convertible with the free, nor extends more widely than it. And accordingly since the will is not borne toward the ultimate end without a full and certain judgment of reason, it is no less freely occupied about it than while it desires the means which seem to lead to that end. Nor do only men living in this life, while they will to be happy, and refuse to be miserable, put forth a free act of the will; but also the blessed themselves in heaven, while with their whole will they cleave to God clearly seen, since in both the will follows in this part a fixed, certain and evident and constantly approved judgment of the intellect, and while it reflects upon itself, it approves that act of its own in the highest degree.
pass_b: On his principles, then, 'voluntary' has two senses.

First, a broader and less proper one, covering every motion that arises in the will in any way at all. In that sense the voluntary is wider than the free, since first-first motions are voluntary but not free.

Second, a strict and proper sense, in which those acts of the will, and only those, are voluntary that occur when reason is attending and has weighed the matter and judged it. Taken so, the voluntary and the free coincide, and the one is no wider than the other.
Since the will does not move toward the last end without a full and sure judgment of reason, it acts no less freely regarding that end than when it seeks the means that seem to lead there.

So it is not only people in this life who perform a free act of will when they want to be happy and not miserable. The blessed in heaven do so too when they cling with their whole will to God whom they see clearly. In both cases the will here follows a firm, certain, evident, and steadily approved judgment of the intellect, and when it reflects on itself it approves that act of its own to the utmost.

lemmas.gloss: the voluntary is convertible with the free

sections.title: Jansenius: indifference is not of the essence of freedom; freedom is the agent's mastery of itself
sections.pass_a: For he does not think that to the common character of liberty, and its proper essence, there pertains a certain indifference and indetermination of the will in respect of the act which is called free, by which the will can do the contrary, or at least omit or suspend that act. For in his mind, liberty consists only in this, that the free agent is master of itself and of its act, and acts and moves itself, but is not acted on and moved by another, which he contends holds place even in those acts to which the will is determined necessarily and immutably.
pass_b: He does not hold that the general character and proper essence of freedom includes any indifference or indeterminacy of the will toward the act called free, such that the will could do the opposite, or at least leave the act undone or hold it back.

In his view freedom consists only in this: the free agent rules itself and its act, and it acts and moves itself rather than being acted on and moved by another. He maintains that this holds even in acts to which the will is fixed necessarily and unchangeably.

sections.title: Jansenius with Scotus: the necessity in such acts is concomitant, not antecedent
sections.pass_a: For the necessity which is then found in the will, as he expresses his mind in the words of Scotus, is not prior to the will, so that the will is understood to fall under necessity, as impelling into the act, and fixing in the act, since if it were so, the will would be acted on and would not act, nor would liberty stand in such an act. But it is a concomitant necessity, so that it is understood to fall under the will, so that the will, because of the firmness of its liberty, imposes necessity on itself in eliciting the act, and in persevering, or fixing, itself in the act. On the Grace of Christ the Saviour book 6. chap. 37.
pass_b: The necessity then present in the will, as he puts it in Scotus's words, 'does not come before the will, so that the will would be understood to fall under a necessity that drives it into the act and fixes it there. If that were so, the will would be acted upon and would not act, and freedom could not remain in such an act.

'It is a concomitant necessity, understood to fall under the will. The will, through the firmness of its freedom, lays necessity on itself in bringing forth its act and in persevering in it, that is, in fixing itself on the act.' (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 37.)

sections.title: Jansenius: reason and will reflect on their own acts, so the rational agent always moves itself
sections.pass_a: And to show more clearly that the rational agent in all things which it wills and desires in a certain way acts and moves itself, although the act of its will be necessary and immutable, he observes that the power of acting and moving oneself, which is proper to the free agent, is placed in this, that both reason and will, to which faculties liberty pertains, can reflect upon their acts; so that reason can judge of its own judgment, whether it has judged rightly; and likewise the will can not only will and desire, but also will its very volition, and its desire. And because in every rational motion, whether it be necessary, or not necessary, such reflexion upon itself is always present tacitly, or expressly, always also in every motion of its own the rational agent moves itself and is master of itself, and so exercises its proper liberty.
pass_b: To show more plainly that a rational agent in some way acts and moves itself in everything it wills and desires, even when its act of will is necessary and unchangeable, he observes where the power of self-action and self-movement lies, the power that belongs to a free agent.

It lies in the fact that both reason and will, the faculties to which freedom belongs, can turn back on their own acts. Reason can judge its own judgment and ask whether it judged rightly. The will likewise can not only will and desire but also will its own willing and its own desire.

In every rational motion, necessary or not, such reflection on itself is always present, silently or openly. So in every motion a rational agent always moves itself and is master of itself, and in this way exercises its own freedom.

sections.title: Jansenius: the blessed love God most freely; their necessity comes from the perfection of their freedom
sections.pass_a: For according to him, the proper marks of true liberty are to do what pleases the agent, what is agreeable to him, what seems good to him. Whence he gathers that the Blessed in heaven, in loving God whom they clearly see, most perfectly move themselves, and have the most perfect dominion of their act, and so are most free, because with a most full and most tranquil judgment they judge that God is to be loved by them, and judge that they judge most soundly in this; but their will in loving wills to follow reason, and wills that it wills this, and does not will to cease. But the necessity which appears in that act proceeds from the will itself, and from the perfection of its Dominion and liberty, because it makes necessity for itself, not by way of nature, but of the most perfect liberty, by moving and determining itself.
pass_b: In his account the proper signs of true freedom are doing what the agent likes, what pleases him, what seems good to him.

From this he concludes that the blessed in heaven, loving the God they see clearly, move themselves most perfectly, hold the most perfect command over their act, and so are supremely free. With the fullest and calmest judgment they judge that God must be loved by them, and they judge that in this they judge most soundly. Their will, in loving, wants to follow reason, wants to want this, and does not want to stop.

Whatever necessity shows in that act comes from the will itself and from the perfection of its mastery and freedom. The will creates that necessity for itself by moving and determining itself, not in the manner of nature but in the manner of the most perfect freedom.

sections.title: Jansenius grants wayfarers indifference but makes it a sign of freedom, not its cause
sections.pass_a: However although that Doctor will not have it pertain to the proper essence of liberty that the will hold itself indifferently toward its acts, so namely that it can act, and not act, do this or also the contrary; yet with the old Scholastics he openly confesses that such indifference is present in the will of men who are wayfarers; for their liberty is free not only from compulsion, but also from voluntary immutable necessity, that is, it is indifferent to either. This only he denies, that the general liberty of human choice is placed in that indifference. For this indifference is indeed a most certain mark of liberty in a rational creature, yet not the cause, or reason, of liberty. And therefore it can be present or absent at the choice of the will, without loss of liberty. On the Grace of Christ the Saviour book 6. chap. 34.
pass_b: That teacher will not have it belong to the proper essence of freedom that the will stand indifferently toward its acts, able to act or not act, to do this or even its opposite.

Yet with the old scholastics he openly admits that such indifference is present in the will of people still on their earthly way. Their freedom is exempt not only from compulsion but also from unchangeable voluntary necessity; it is open to either side.

What he denies is only that the general freedom of human choice consists in that indifference. The indifference is indeed a most certain sign of freedom in a rational creature, but it is not the cause or ground of freedom. It can therefore be present or absent at the will's discretion without any loss of freedom. (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 34.)

sections.title: The Jansenists' Manuale Catholicorum: freedom does not consist in indifference
sections.pass_a: And this doctrine of Jansenius they have embraced, and still embrace, who call themselves disciples of Augustine, and are called Jansenists by their adversaries, as may be seen in the book to which they gave the title Manual of Catholics, in the twenty-first Apologetic and dogmatic Thesis. Where these are their words, The essence of liberty in no way consists in indifference. For from the Holy Fathers, Where the will is there is liberty. For Free Choice is, from Saint Prosper, the Spontaneous appetite of a thing pleasing to oneself. And from St. Damascene The Liberty of Choice is nothing else than the will. And a little after, What is done voluntarily, even if it be done necessarily, is yet done freely. For God loves himself necessarily, and yet freely. Likewise, therefore only the necessity of compulsion, or of violence, is repugnant to Liberty, but not simple necessity, immutable, or of natural inclination.
pass_b: Those who call themselves disciples of Augustine, and whom their opponents call Jansenists, took up this doctrine of Jansenius and still hold it. This can be seen in their book entitled Manual of Catholics, in the twenty-first apologetic and doctrinal thesis.

They write there: 'The essence of freedom in no way consists in indifference. For the holy Fathers say, Where there is will, there is freedom. Free choice, according to St Prosper, is the spontaneous appetite for a thing that pleases one. And according to St John of Damascus, freedom of choice is nothing other than the will.'

A little later they add: 'What is done voluntarily is done freely, even if it is done necessarily, for God loves himself necessarily and yet freely.' And again: 'Only the necessity of compulsion or violence, then, is incompatible with freedom, not simple necessity, unchangeable necessity, or the necessity of natural inclination.'

notes: Manuale Catholicorum, apologetic and dogmatic thesis 21; the patristic sayings are as the Manual gives them.

sections.title: The 'three columns': Jansenists accept a sense of the third condemned proposition, yet require freedom from necessity
sections.pass_a: But in that writing which they call of the three columns, where they distinguish the various senses of the five famous propositions which the Roman Pontiffs Innocent X. and Alexander VII. condemned, to the third proposition they attribute this sense as good and approved by them. For meriting and demeriting, in the state of fallen nature, there is not required in man liberty from the necessity of infallibility, but Liberty from compulsion with the judgment of reason suffices, if the essence of liberty and merit be considered precisely, although by reason of the state there is always found an indifference of power, by which the will, even under grace proximately necessary and of itself efficacious, can not will, yet not so that it ever at the same time with the same grace does not will. Where they acknowledge that always in the state of fallen nature, indifference of the will is joined to Liberty. And therefore in those articles offered to the Bishop of Comminges, they do not fear to say, That for meriting and demeriting in the state of fallen nature Liberty from compulsion does not suffice; but liberty from necessity is required. For although, they say, grace efficacious of itself infallibly and insuperably determines the will to act, and so the will never in act dissents from it; yet it does not induce necessity, because it does not take away the power of dissenting.
pass_b: In the paper they call 'of the three columns', where they separate the different senses of the five well-known propositions condemned by the popes Innocent X and Alexander VII, they assign to the third proposition the following sense as sound and accepted by them.

'To merit and demerit in the state of fallen nature, man does not need freedom from the necessity of infallibility. Freedom from compulsion together with the judgment of reason is enough, if one considers strictly the essence of freedom and of merit. Yet given the condition of that state, there is always an indifference of power by which the will, even under grace that is proximately necessary and efficacious of itself, is able not to will, though never so as not to will while under that same grace.'
Here they grant that in the state of fallen nature indifference of the will always goes with freedom.

That is why, in the articles presented to the bishop of Comminges, they do not hesitate to say: 'To merit and demerit in the state of fallen nature, freedom from compulsion is not enough; freedom from necessity is required. For although grace efficacious of itself determines the will to act infallibly and irresistibly, so that the will never actually dissents from it, it does not bring in necessity, since it does not remove the power of dissenting.'

notes: The 'three columns' paper set the five propositions condemned by Innocent X (Cum occasione, 1653) and Alexander VII beside their admissible and inadmissible senses; Convenae is Comminges.

sections.title: Rome condemned the view that freedom is opposed to compulsion only: Pius V and Gregory XIII
sections.pass_a: But that opinion which states liberty of choice to be opposed, not to necessity, but to compulsion only, has been condemned by the Roman Pontiffs. For Bellarmine mentions a certain decree of Pius V. which was afterwards renewed by Gregory XIII. in which among many other propositions, these also are marked with censure. What is done voluntarily, even if it be done by necessity, is yet done freely. Likewise, violence alone is repugnant to the natural liberty of man.
pass_b: The view that freedom of choice is opposed only to compulsion and not to necessity has, however, been condemned by the popes of Rome.

Bellarmine mentions a decree of Pius V, later renewed by Gregory XIII, which censures these two propositions among many others: 'What is done voluntarily is done freely, even if it is done of necessity', and 'Only violence is incompatible with man's natural freedom.'

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.

notes: The decree is Pius V's bull Ex omnibus afflictionibus (1567) against Baius, confirmed by Gregory XIII (Provisionis nostrae, 1579); Le Blanc names neither bull; these are Baius's propositions 39 and 66.

sections.title: Common Roman doctrine now: freedom requires immunity from necessity, at least absolute and natural
sections.pass_a: Therefore the common doctrine of the Roman School today is, that for liberty of choice immunity from compulsion alone does not suffice, but besides there is required immunity from necessity, at least absolute and natural, by which things are by nature determined to one thing, and simply cannot act otherwise than they act. And in this head agree both those who are called the more recent Thomists, and those called Molinists.
pass_b: The common teaching of the Roman School today, then, is that freedom from compulsion is not enough for freedom of choice. There must also be freedom from necessity, at least from absolute and natural necessity, the kind by which things are fixed by nature on one course and simply cannot act otherwise than they do.
On this point both the more recent Thomists and the Molinists agree.

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.

sections.title: Hence the voluntary is a genus with two species, and the spontaneous a wider genus still
sections.pass_a: Therefore they will not have what is voluntary be free, if the will be necessarily determined to it, as the will of the Blessed Spirits to loving God whom they clearly see. And accordingly they conceive the voluntary as a certain genus, which embraces under itself two species, namely the free which is done with selection and preference, and the voluntary strictly and properly so called, which is done indeed willingly, yet not freely; because necessarily and immutably. But they make the spontaneous the genus of the voluntary, since not only those things which are endowed with intellect and will act spontaneously, but also brutes which lack reason. Nay even inanimate things themselves, as a stone when it tends downward. For to act spontaneously is to act by the impulse of nature.
pass_b: They therefore deny that what is voluntary is free when the will is necessarily fixed on it, as the will of the blessed spirits is fixed on loving the God they see clearly.

So they treat the voluntary as a genus with two species under it. One is the free, which is done with selection and preference. The other is the voluntary in the strict and proper sense, which is done gladly but not freely, because it is done necessarily and unchangeably.

Above the voluntary they place the spontaneous as its genus. For not only beings with intellect and will act of their own accord, but also brute animals without reason, and even lifeless things, such as a stone moving downward, since acting spontaneously means acting on nature's impulse.

sections.title: They distinguish willingness or complacency from liberty, which is of contrariety or of contradiction
sections.pass_a: Therefore they distinguish willingness, or complacency from liberty: nor will they have any liberty properly so called, except that which is either of contrariety, or of specification, by which one can elicit contrary acts about the same object, or desire objects contrary or disparate. Or at least of contradiction, or of exercise, by which one can act, and suspend, or inhibit his action.
pass_b: They thus separate willingness, or complacency, from freedom. They allow no freedom in the proper sense except two kinds.

One is freedom of contrariety or specification, by which a person can produce opposite acts toward the same object, or seek objects that are opposed or simply different. The other, at the least, is freedom of contradiction or exercise, by which a person can act and also hold back or check his action.

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.

sections.title: They require indifference and indetermination: the common description of freedom
sections.pass_a: For they will not have liberty to be without a certain indifference and indetermination of the free agent to acting; and they think those acts alone free whose contrary we can do, or at least omit them, and cease from them: according to that common description of liberty, by which it is said to consist in this, that the free agent, all prerequisites for acting being posited, can act, or not act, do this, or that.
pass_b: They do not allow freedom without some indifference and indeterminacy in the free agent with respect to acting. Only those acts are free, they think, whose opposite we can do, or which we can at least leave undone and break off.
This follows the familiar description of freedom, which places it in this: given everything required beforehand for acting, the free agent can act or not act, and can do this or that.

lemmas.gloss: all prerequisites for acting being posited

sections.title: Some recent Thomists make indifference a property of freedom, its essence independence and dominion
sections.pass_a: Yet some recent Thomists observe that indifference to acting, or not acting, is indeed a property of human liberty, which cannot be separated from it; but that the essence of liberty does not consist in it; but rather in independence, and eminence above finite goods, and in that force of ruling; or in a certain dominion, by which it refers itself and its own to the ultimate end. As may be seen in the recent writer Vincent Baron the Dominican in the third part of dogmatic Theology; on the principles of human Liberty and of the knowledge of God against Theophile Raynaud the Jesuit. Disp. 1. Artic. 3. §. 1. But according to the more common positions of the present School, the very essence of liberty is to be placed in this indifference to acting, or not acting.
pass_b: Some recent Thomists, however, note that indifference toward acting or not acting is a property of human freedom that cannot be separated from it, but that the essence of freedom does not lie there.

They place it rather in independence and in standing above finite goods, together with the power of governing, or in a kind of dominion by which the free agent directs itself and all that is its own to the last end.

This can be seen in the recent Dominican writer Vincent Baron, in the third part of his dogmatic theology, on the principles of human freedom and of God's knowledge, written against the Jesuit Théophile Raynaud (disputation 1, article 3, §1).
Yet by the more common positions of today's school, the very essence of freedom is to be placed in this indifference toward acting or not acting.

lemmas.gloss: independence, and eminence above finite goods

notes: Vincent Baron OP, the Dominican; not the Reformed Robert Baron cited elsewhere in the theses.

sections.title: The indifference they mean is not equilibrium but the real power of acting and not acting
sections.pass_a: Further, the Doctors of the Roman Church by that indifference which either constitutes the essence of liberty, or at least necessarily follows it, do not wish to signify that state of the will in which it wavers between two opposites, and inclines no more to one than to the other; but suspended in a certain way in equilibrium, is driven hither and thither by a slight weight. For they acknowledge liberty to be found in him who in that sense is not at all indifferent to acting; but whose will is vehemently inclined to certain actions by deeply impressed habits, and who has a firm purpose of acting so and not otherwise, from which he cannot be moved except very hardly. But that indifference in which, in their mind, liberty of choice is placed, is nothing else than a true power of acting and not acting, which remains even in him who is determined to acting by a fixed and constant purpose of mind and will.
pass_b: When the teachers of the Roman Church speak of the indifference that either makes up the essence of freedom or at least necessarily goes with it, they do not mean a state in which the will wavers between two opposites, leaning no more to one than to the other, hanging as if in balance and pushed this way and that by the slightest weight.

They grant that freedom is present in someone who is not at all indifferent in that sense. His will may be strongly inclined to certain actions by deeply rooted habits, and he may have a settled purpose of acting this way and no other, from which he can be moved only with great difficulty.

The indifference in which, in their view, freedom of choice lies is nothing else than a real power of acting and not acting. It remains even in someone whose mind and will are fixed on acting by a firm and steady purpose.

lemmas.gloss: a true power of acting and not acting

sections.title: Rome: freedom does not require indifference to good and evil; God, Christ, the angels, the damned
sections.pass_a: Moreover it must be observed, according to the common sense of the Doctors of the Roman Church, that for liberty there is not required indetermination and indifference to acting well, or ill. Nor is it of the essence of liberty to be able to act well, and much less still to be able to act ill. For they acknowledge God to be a most free agent, who yet cannot act ill: as neither could Christ the man ever: nor now can the angels, and heavenly spirits who, by the singular benefit of God, are immutably confirmed in good, nor yet are they on that account less free. But on the contrary, as they confess, the Devils and the Spirits of the damned in hell can do nothing good, and yet act freely, and free choice has remained in them. And that because, although the former are determined to acting well, and the latter on the contrary to acting ill, yet they can abstain from these and those acts, and choose among several goods, or evils. As may be seen in Puteanus on the 1. 2. quest. 10. art. 1, 2, 3, 4. doubt 3. And in William Estius on the 2. of the sentences dist. 14. §. 5.
pass_b: It should also be noted that in the common view of the Roman Church's teachers freedom does not require indeterminacy or indifference between acting well and acting badly. The ability to act well is no part of the essence of freedom, and still less the ability to act badly.

They hold that God is the freest of agents, yet he cannot act badly. Neither could Christ as man at any time. Nor can the angels and heavenly spirits now, who by God's singular favour are unchangeably confirmed in good, and they are none the less free for that.
Conversely, by their own admission, the devils and the spirits of the damned in hell can do nothing good, and yet they act freely and free choice has remained in them.

The reason is that, though the first are fixed on acting well and the second on acting badly, both can refrain from particular acts and choose among several goods or several evils. See Puteanus on the Prima Secundae, q. 10, arts. 1-4, doubt 3, and William Estius on the second book of the Sentences, dist. 14, §5.

notes: Puteanus: presumably Joannes Puteanus (Jean Dupuy) of Toulouse, commentator on the Summa I-II.

sections.title: The formula 'all prerequisites posited, can act and not act': first sense, simultaneity of power not power of simultaneity
sections.pass_a: However that description in which liberty is said to be that by which, all prerequisites for acting being posited, the free agent can act, and not act, do this and that, is not explained in the same sense by all the Theologians of the Roman School. That this may be understood, it must be noted that a manifold sense can be attributed to those words. And first indeed those words can be so taken as if by them it were signified that the free agent can act and not act at once, and at the same time exercise contrary acts. This sense is rejected by all as manifestly false. For all confess that in the free agent act and cessation from act, or one act and its contrary, cannot be compatible at once; and accordingly that by those words nothing else is signified, than that the free agent has at once the power to contrary acts, and that at once there is found in it the power of acting, and the power also of not acting; which in the Schools is said to mean that by this there is attributed to the free agent simultaneity of power, not power of simultaneity.
pass_b: The definition that calls freedom the power by which a free agent, given everything required beforehand for acting, can act and not act, do this and that, is not understood in the same way by every theologian of the Roman School. To see this, note that the words can bear several senses.
First, they could be taken to mean that the free agent can act and not act at once, performing opposite acts at the same moment. Everyone rejects this as plainly false.

All agree that in a free agent an act and the absence of that act, or an act and its opposite, cannot coexist at the same time. They therefore take the words to mean only that the free agent has at one and the same time the power for opposite acts, so that the power of acting and the power of not acting are both found in it together.
The schools express this by saying that what is ascribed to the free agent is simultaneity of power, not power of simultaneity.

lemmas.gloss: simultaneity of power, not power of simultaneity

sections.title: Second sense: with all prerequisites, even divine motion, the act may not follow and its contrary may
sections.pass_a: But secondly this may be the sense of this description, that all things being posited which are prerequired for some act of the free will, both on the part of the object, and on the part of God, and of the intellect itself, that act can as well not follow as follow, and also the contrary act be substituted in its place: so that, although some act and its privation, or contrary act, cannot be compounded and conjoined; yet with all those things which are prerequired for some act of the Human will, for example, of conversion, and of the love of God, there can be joined, and often in fact is joined, the privation of that act, and also the act opposed to it: And so, notwithstanding whatever light of the object, and also allurement, whatever dictate and judgment of the intellect, and lastly whatever divine motion, which impel to conversion, and yet precede the actual determination of the will itself, conversion can really not follow; and it often in fact happens, all these things standing in like manner, that in one indeed they have conversion joined to them, but in another not at all, because the will in the one so determined itself, but in the other otherwise.
pass_b: A second possible sense of the description is this. Given everything required beforehand for some act of the free will, on the side of the object, on the side of God, and on the side of the intellect, that act can just as well not follow as follow, and an opposite act can even take its place.

An act cannot be combined or joined with its own absence or with the opposite act. But all that is required beforehand for some act of the human will, say conversion and the love of God, can be joined with the absence of that act and even with the act opposed to it, and often actually is.

Thus, whatever the light and even the attraction of the object, whatever the dictate and judgment of the intellect, and finally whatever divine motion urges toward conversion while still preceding the will's own actual determination, conversion may in fact not follow.

It often does happen that, with all these things exactly alike, conversion goes with them in one person and not at all in another, because the will determined itself one way in the first and otherwise in the second.

lemmas.gloss: the actual determination of the will itself

sections.title: The Molinists accept the second sense: the composed sense true of the prerequisites, false of the act
sections.pass_a: And this sense is approved and admitted by those who in the Roman School are called Molinists. For they will not have there be anything of those things which, both on the part of God and on the part of the intellect, prepare the human will for consent, and antecedently move and impel it, with which the dissent of the will cannot stand. And they lay down that any judgment of reason whatever, and also any divine motion whatever, can be compounded, not only with the act to which they premove and direct the will, but also with the lack of that act, nay with the contrary act: so that the same motion of divine grace works conversion to God in one, but in another not: because the one willed of his own accord to follow the leading of divine grace, but the other not at all. And so in a different respect they both deny and affirm that the free agent, all requisites for acting being posited, can, in the composed sense, act and not act, do this and that. For if anyone understand that in the free agent there can be compounded act and cessation from act, one act and its opposite, they confess that composed sense to be false, and only the divided sense, which is opposed to it, true. But if anyone maintain that not indeed with the act itself, but yet with all the requisites for acting, there can be compounded the privation of the act, and the opposite act, that composed sense, according to them, is true.
pass_b: This sense is approved and accepted by those in the Roman School called Molinists. They deny that anything which prepares the human will for consent and moves and drives it beforehand, whether on God's side or on the intellect's, is incompatible with the will's dissent.

They hold that any judgment of reason and even any divine motion can be combined not only with the act toward which they move and direct the will in advance, but also with the absence of that act, and indeed with the contrary act. So the same motion of divine grace brings about conversion to God in one person and not in another, because the first chose of his own accord to follow grace's leading and the second did not.
In different respects, then, they both deny and affirm that the free agent, given all that is required for acting, can act and not act, do this and that, in the composed sense.

If it is taken to mean that in the free agent an act can be combined with ceasing from it, or one act with its opposite, they grant that this composed sense is false and only the divided sense opposed to it is true. But if someone holds that the absence of the act, or the opposite act, can be combined not with the act itself but with all that is required for acting, then in their view that composed sense is true.

sections.title: The recent Thomists deny both composed senses yet keep the power of not acting, as one sitting can walk
sections.pass_a: But otherwise think those who are called the more recent Thomists. For according to their doctrine, each of those composed senses is false. Since they think that not only can its privation, or the opposite act, not be joined with the act; but that not even with those things which are prerequisite for acting, among which a certain divine premotion has place, can the negation of the act consist, and much less the contrary act. And that because when the things are posited which are prerequired for some act, that act follows certainly and infallibly; nor can it ever happen that it does not follow. And yet they grant that, all prerequisites for acting being posited, the free agent can act, and not act, do this and that: because although with those prerequisites the negation of the act, or the suspension of the act, cannot stand; yet with them the power of not acting, or also of acting contrarily, consists excellently. Not otherwise than with the actual consent of the will the dissent of the will indeed cannot stand, but yet the very power of dissenting remains: And with the act of sitting the act of walking cannot be compatible, although the power of walking is not repugnant to it, which in one sitting is not taken away by the act of sitting. In that way therefore the prerequisites for acting, both on the part of God, and on the part of our intellect, draw the act itself with them by necessary consequence, and yet by no means take away the power of not acting. Since they bring about indeed that the will acts, but yet so acts, that it can not act, and does not lose the power of acting otherwise.
pass_b: Those called the more recent Thomists think differently, for on their teaching both composed senses are false.

They hold that an act cannot be joined with its own absence or with the opposite act. Nor can the absence of the act, much less the contrary act, coexist with what is required beforehand for acting, among which is a certain divine premotion. Once what is required for an act is in place, the act follows certainly and infallibly, and it can never happen that it does not follow.

Yet they grant that, given all that is required for acting, the free agent can act and not act, do this and that. Though the absence or suspension of the act cannot stand with those prerequisites, the power of not acting, or of acting in the contrary way, fits with them perfectly well.

It is just as when the will actually consents: dissent cannot stand with that consent, but the power of dissenting remains. Again, the act of walking cannot go with the act of sitting, yet the power of walking does not conflict with it, and sitting does not remove that power from the one who sits.

In the same way the prerequisites for acting, whether on God's side or on the side of our intellect, carry the act along with them by necessary consequence, yet in no way remove the power of not acting. They do make the will act, but so that it acts while still able not to act, and without losing the power to act otherwise.

sections.title: Diego Alvarez states the Thomist view and its definition of free choice
sections.pass_a: Thus Diego Alvarez, Archbishop of Trani and Salpi, chief among the more recent Thomists, sets out his mind on this matter. It must be said, he says, that for liberty of choice it is necessarily required that, all things being posited antecedently prerequisite to the act according to the order of reason or of time, it can operate, or not operate, namely so, that with the same prerequisites there stands at once in free choice the faculty and power, by which it can operate, or not operate, if it will. And it is proved, For if any of the prerequisites for operating such an act in particular took away from free choice the faculty, or power for not operating, or for operating the opposite act; this would be done by the efficacious motion of God, by which it is predetermined to such an act: but such motion does not take away from free choice the faculty of not operating that act, or of operating the contrary act, but only brings about that, since free choice can operate, and not operate such an act; it yet operates it infallibly and freely.... Yet it is not of the nature, or definition of free choice, that, all things being posited antecedently prerequisite according to the order of causality, for operating such an act, it can not operate the same act in the composed sense, if the composition be made between such prerequisites, and the lack of such act, or the contrary act. Therefore these two are at once incompossible, namely, that in free choice, for some instant of time, all things antecedently prerequisite according to the order of causality, for the production of such act, be present, and it not produce it but produce the contrary act. And nevertheless with this impossibility the liberty of choice stands at once. In the summary of the work on the aids of Divine grace book 4. chap. 14. num. 5. and 6. And therefore to avoid all equivocation, this is, according to him, the legitimate definition of free choice, free choice is the faculty of will, and reason for doing either, or not doing, and doing one thing, or another.
pass_b: Diego Alvarez, archbishop of Trani and Salpi and the leading figure among the more recent Thomists, explains his view as follows.

'It must be held that freedom of choice necessarily requires this: given everything required before the act, whether in order of reason or of time, it can act or not act. That is, together with those same prerequisites there is present in free choice the faculty and power by which it can act or not act, if it wishes.

'The proof is this. If any of the things required for performing a given act took from free choice the faculty or power of not acting, or of performing the opposite act, it would be God's efficacious motion by which free choice is predetermined to that act. But such motion does not remove the faculty of not performing that act or of performing the contrary one. It brings about only this: free choice, though able to perform the act or not, does in fact perform it infallibly and freely...

'Yet it is not part of the nature or definition of free choice that, given all that is required in advance in the order of causality for performing a given act, it can leave that same act undone in the composed sense, if the composition is made between those prerequisites and the absence of that act, or the contrary act.

'So these two things cannot coexist: that in free choice, at some instant of time, all that is required in advance in the order of causality for producing a given act is present, and yet it does not produce that act but produces the contrary. And freedom of choice nevertheless stands together with this impossibility.' (Summary of the work on the aids of divine grace, book 4, chapter 14, nos. 5 and 6.)

To avoid all ambiguity, then, the proper definition of free choice on his account is: 'Free choice is the faculty of will and reason for acting or not acting, either way, and for doing one thing or another.'
